Catastrophe risk modelling specialist Karen Clark & Company (KCC) has provided an initial estimate for the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias, saying it expects the total to be $3 billion.

KCC said that its industry loss estimate includes privately insured damages to residential, commercial, and industrial properties and automobiles, as well as business interruption, but does not include boats, offshore properties, or losses to the NFIP flood policies.

This latest estimate for the recent hurricane impacts on the Gulf Coast can be compared to one from Verisk, which recently gave its initial industry insured loss estimate for Isaias, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion.

In addition, Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion.

Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range.

KCC commented on the impacts of the hurricane, “Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, FL as a Category 2 hurricane with 105-mph maximum sustained winds and a peak storm surge of about 8 feet. The most severe impacts were concentrated in the coastal cities and towns of the Florida Panhandle, like Destin, Pensacola Beach, and Navarre. Major damage has also been observed in towns around Pensacola Bay, such as Milton and Pace.

“Many downed trees and severe structural damage to buildings were reported in the town of Milton, FL, which is about 20 miles inland from the Panhandle coast. Partial and total pull out of roofs were observed in both residential and commercial properties, including single family homes, multi-family homes, motels, and grocery stores.

“Some mid-rise and high-rise buildings in Pensacola Beach have sustained damage to wall sidings and cladding. Many gas stations in the beach towns have been destroyed. Power outages were widespread across Florida and Alabama and extended into western Georgia where winds from the outer bands of Isaias caused many fallen tree limbs.”

Also, reinsurance broker Gallagher Re has reaffirmed its loss estimate, saying it now expects hurricane Isaias’ industry losses will fall in the lower end of the low to mid-single-digit billions of dollars range.

In addition, rating agency AM Best said today that, “insured loss estimates are expected to be in the low single digit range in billions of dollars.”

AM Best added that the hurricane will likely have minimal macro impact on reinsurance renewals, saying, “reinsurance capacity and pricing is not expected to be dramatically impacted.”

Speaking yesterday at the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference, Bob Smith, President & Co-CIO of fixed income and alternative solutions manager Sage Advisory, explained that he sees insurance-linked securities as an asset class that can expand the horizon of impact investing.

Smith is a strong proponent for investing into catastrophe bonds and other natural catastrophe linked insurance-linked securities, seeing them as particularly valuable diversifiers that over the long-term have also outperformed many other fixed income asset classes.

But, as well as the low-correlation and differentiated return features that cat bonds and ILS can bring to investors portfolios, Smith also believes strongly in the sustainable investment qualities of the asset class.

“In this environment, one of the things that we always look for, because we are in many ways a sustainably focused investor as well at our firm, and we believe in responsible investing. So we’re always looking for investments that have impact and if there’s anything I can tell you at this conference, is indeed cat ILS is an impact investment,” Smith explained.

“It has economic purpose. There’s a lot of stuff in the asset backed world where I’m not really sure I get the economic purpose, other than what the management wants. Is it really good for the broader economy and society?”

Smith went on to say, “When we look at investments, we want to also be socially engaged. I think that ILS, quite frankly, needs to be front and centre in most impact portfolios.

“It’s an area that’s completely missed in terms of investors, and the problem with most impact investing is that it’s all about mitigation. But when we talk about this area, cat ILS, we’re talking about investing in resiliency, and resiliency is the number one byproduct of the effort in ILS.

“Yes, there is economic purpose, but we’re really about adaptation not mitigation. We’re about economic stability, and lastly, social risk. We want to make sure society continues on, and that there is not unrest.

“So, through the mechanism and the risk transfer mechanism offered by ILS, I think you expand the horizon for impact investing, and I think that is where the focus needs to be, because there’s a lot of money out there looking for this product, looking for this area of the market to invest in.”

You can read more of the firm’s thoughts on the impact topic in this article: ILS & cat bonds show impact investing can move beyond mitigation into resilience: Sage Advisory.

For investors in the insurance-linked securities asset class, when pitching a potential allocation to their investment committees the task is helped by the fact ILS has a strong narrative to tell, when it comes to proving its diversification benefits and has the data to support that, speakers at the Convergence 2026 conference in Bermuda said today.

During a panel discussion at the event featuring end-investor allocators and an investment firm that provides specialist advisory and portfolio construction services, the speakers explained that while it’s not always the easiest asset class to present to an investment committee, the fact ILS has the data to evidence the diversification story is helpful.

Joe Tolen, Senior Investment Director at specialist advisor Cambridge Associates, said that explaining the true diversification benefits of some private and alternative asset classes can be a challenge, but when it comes to insurance-linked securities there is an easier story to tell.

“I think that’s a super-important point and something people in this room should try to build on, is that proof of diversification. Because I’ve struggled with it in my uncorrelated credit branding of trying to show certain pockets of litigation finance, and you can anecdotally tell someone that the returns of a law firm lending strategy is based on a diversified pool of fee receivables that have nothing to do with central bank policy or corporate earnings GDP growth. You can tell them that, but because all the strategies are private, it’s very difficult to show them that,” Tolen explained.

He added, “So I think ILS really has an upper-edge, in having the data available and being able to prove that diversification.

“With ILS specifically, I think diversification is the major selling point. It’s what gets people to pay attention, and it’s what gets them at the table.”

Scott Radke, CEO & Co-CIO, New Holland Capital, an allocator to the insurance-linked securities asset class, commented, “I think it starts with a governance situation. So trustees or a board and CIO that’s open to innovation, or at least not opposed to it, so there’s a climate which is receptive to these kinds of somewhat unorthodox ideas.

“Then it’s an organisation which is focused on portfolio construction, so they think about it through that lens, and as a result, can appreciate the value of the diversification that something like ILS offers. ”

Nidhi Sharma, Director & Senior Portfolio Manager – Alpha Alternatives, PSP Investments (another allocator), further explained, “I actually think ILS has a very strong narrative as an asset class. The lack of correlation is, I think, probably the most intuitive, strongest to prove out. It has a decent history of data and indices that you could check that against. The liquidity is actually really attractive, it’s short duration, it fits in the portfolio. There’s enough scale, it’s a market that has continued to grow and evolve, and you have different flavours of executing in this for different structures.

“I actually think that if you’re a long-term investor who will accept that there will be drawdowns and losses in certain years, which is the case with every single asset class, and that you can weather that kind of volatility, and that’s a portfolio construction question, then I think it’s easy to make the case.”

The panel also discussed the fact that, for investment professionals presenting the asset class to their boards there can be an element of career risk, in championing an investment strategy that continues to be considered novel at many investment committees.

Something that the availability of data to provide examples of the potential upside and downside can also assist with.

Radke commented, “To get to the finish line, you need a champion, and the champion isn’t the CIO. The champion’s the mid-level person who decides to make a run at it, probably you know in some ways unwisely at least initially, where they’re taking a little bit of career risk.”

Sharma added, “My impression is that ILS is easy to like, it’s hard to understand the risk. You have a lot of models that will tell you what happens in the worst 1% of outcomes, the worst 10% of outcomes. But, I think ultimately, sitting in an IC, looking at the people around and telling them that if you have Hurricane Katrina today, and if it goes through Miami, Philadelphia, and New York, you are looking to lose pretty much all of your capital, and that is the worst-case scenario. Are you comfortable with that? That’s where the question of enthusiasm, career risk actually comes in and I think having that candid conversation and telling people that this is what you’re finally signing up to, that in this scenario you can lose this much money and do you have that actual willingness to lose, then of course I think the pathway is clear. And if not, then either it’s a no, or scale back, or right size.”

Tolen further stated, “I think you both bringing up career risk is super important, but it depends on the investment knowledge of the IC as well, especially at a lot of public pension plans. For instance, that IC, that board they might not be made up of investment professionals, which can make it a little bit scary from a behavioural economic standpoint to back an industry that has the word catastrophe in one of their products.

“I think it’s a lot easier for them to just think, oh, you know what I would rather go down the more conventional route and potentially leave something on the table than enter into something where it could be another Katrina and it could be six months after you invest, and all of a sudden you have egg on your face, and you’re getting questions about why did you allocate it to this space. So it can be really challenging from from a career standpoint.”

Sharma added, “I can second that by saying, it’s a lot easier to present a music catalogue that everybody’s heard and can find their favourites in, versus something that is a cat bond.”

Given that catastrophe bonds are known for having a low correlation to traditional financial markets, global asset management firm Victory Capital has highlighted how the asset class’s portfolio implementation flexibility makes it viable for either an investor’s fixed income allocation or its alternative investment strategy.

In a recent article, Victory Capital outlines that many investors prioritise the incorporation of strategies with returns that either have low or no correlation to other major asset classes, along with securing new sources of income that have the potential to generate attractive risk-adjusted returns regardless of what’s happening across the broader financial market.

This is where the use of catastrophe bonds, a core component of the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market can play a crucial role.

As Artemis’ readers are aware, the cat bond market has gained heavy momentum in recent years, as organisations have become more familiar with the asset class, which in turn has led to a record influx of new sponsors venturing into the space.

While catastrophe bonds carry event-driven principal risk, Victory Capital importantly highlights that history has shown that investors who deploy cat bonds as a strategic allocation, have not suffered sustained principal losses.

“The insurance industry has demonstrated the ability to reprice risk efficiently (i.e., raise premiums), particularly after a catastrophic event. Thus, we think that the true risk profile of cat bonds is one of the misunderstood aspects of this fixed income asset class,” Victory Capital explained.

Further backing this claim, Victory Capital highlights that the Swiss Re Global Cat Bond Index has managed to deliver a positive performance throughout 18 of the past 19 years.

The firm also underscored how catastrophe bonds as represented by the Swiss Re Global Cat Bond Index, have offered more attractive risk/return characteristics than many more well-known asset classes have throughout the past decade.

“Using the return history of Swiss Re Global Cat Bond Index (2007-2025) as a proxy for the asset class, we evaluated its three-year annualized rolling returns since inception. The range of outcomes were from 2.58% to 16.07%. In 100% (17 of 17) of the rolling three-year periods, the index achieved absolute positive returns, and in all rolling three periods, the returns were in excess of 2%. Of course, past performance does not guarantee future results,” Victory Capital added.

The asset management firm also notes that while financial markets are heavily focused on areas such as inflation data, corporate earnings, tariffs, geopolitics and gross domestic product projections, cat bond investors are much less concerned by these economic metrics, given that they are largely uninfluenced by such factors, and therefore have a low correlation compared to other broad asset classes.

However, the firm warns that much like any investment, there are risks that investors must consider when venturing into the cat bond market.

“A cat bond investment could suffer principal losses upon the occurrence of one or more natural disasters that trigger losses of a certain magnitude. Thus, cat bonds may not be suitable for every investor’s portfolio,” Victory Capital said.

“However, an actively managed cat bond portfolio is designed to balance geographic exposures, while also exploiting possible structural inefficiencies in the market,” the firm added.

Concluding: “In the end, we believe that a cat bond allocation may be well positioned to help solve for several investor objectives. The sources of risk, return, and liquidity are unlike anything in a traditional diversified investment portfolio, and the portfolio implementation flexibility could make them viable for either an investor’s fixed income allocation or an alternative investment bucket.”

PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under its Great Wall Re Limited special purpose insurer is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese Mainland.

Given the limited information, we were incorrect in initially reporting that the new Great Wall Re issuance we had learned about was a catastrophe bond, having made the assumption it was a follow-up to PICC Property and Casualty Company’s debut sponsorship back in late 2022, the $32.5 million Great Wall Re Limited cat bond deal.

PICC Property and Casualty Company has instead utilised Hong Kong’s insurance-linked securities regulatory regime to become the first collateralised reinsurance sidecar sponsor to use an SPI located there.

We had reported on October 5th that a new Great Wall Re issuance of insurance-linked securities had been completed, assuming it to be another cat bond from the sponsor, then following up a few days later after we learned it was a US $12 million (HK $94m) issuance of notes.

Now, it’s clear that this is a landmark first quota share reinsurance sidecar securitisation for Hong Kong, as the country successfully expands the use-cases for its ILS infrastructure.

This morning PICC Property and Casualty Company has said that the US $12 million (HK $94m) Great Wall Re ILS issuance is “the first issuance of insurance-linked securities with a “sidecar” structure in the Hong Kong market,” and the first issuance of sidecar insurance-linked securities by any domestic Chinese insurance company.

It’s a relatively unique deal as well given it provides reinsurance to both PICC People’s Insurance and Property Insurance covering offshore wind power property risks in mainland China, certainly an infrequently seen risk profile for the ILS market, perhaps the first time the market has seen these risks in ILS form.

The insurer said this is “another innovative practice for the company to use the international capital market to spread insurance risks after the successful issuance of disaster bonds in Hong Kong in 2022.”

Being a sidecar, the underlying subject reinsurance arrangement with this US $12 million Great Wall Re deal is a quota share, or proportional reinsurance, transferring the risks to capital market investors on that basis.

The Hong Kong based SPI raises capital to fund the risks by issuing equity or debt securities, with those funds deposited in trust accounts and invested in low-risk, highly liquid assets, paying the investors backed the deal over-time. The income and loss of the insurance-linked securities are linked to the profit and loss of the sidecar’s proportional reinsurance contracts.

PICC P&C explained, “Its issuance structure reflects the core characteristics of income sharing, risk sharing and flexible loading and unloading between insurance companies and capital market investors, so it is called “sidecar”. The “sidecar” insurance-linked securities and disaster bonds that spread risks through super-compensation reinsurance complement each other, which provides new tools for Chinese insurance companies to expand risk diversification channels and enhance underwriting capabilities.”

PICC P&C further stated, “This issue introduces the risk of China’s offshore wind power insurance into the international capital market, enhances international investors’ understanding of China’s green energy insurance business, and expands the risk diversification channel for the development of green energy for insurance services.

“The insurance-linked securities previously issued in the Hong Kong market are all disaster bond structures. This “sidecar” issuance enriches the transaction structure and business scenario of the Hong Kong insurance-linked securities market, which helps to promote the coordinated development of the Hong Kong insurance market, capital market and professional service institutions, and helps improve the Hong Kong International Financial Center. Function, improve the global competitiveness of Hong Kong International Financial Center, and inject new momentum into the financial innovation of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.

“In the next step, People’s Insurance and Property Insurance will continue to practice political and people’s requirements, coordinate development and security, deepen the exploration of insurance risk securitization, continuously broaden the risk dispersion channels, improve the risk protection capacity of large disasters, and contribute to the construction of the national disaster risk protection system and the construction of the Hong Kong International Financial Center.”

Hong Kong’s Financial Services & Treasury Bureau said that it “welcomed the inaugural issuance of insurance-linked securities (ILS) in the form of a “sidecar” by the PICC Property & Casualty Company (PICC P&C) in Hong Kong.”

Secretary for Financial Services & the Treasury Christopher Hui commented, “We welcome PICC P&C’s issuance of Hong Kong’s first ‘sidecar’. This demonstrates Hong Kong’s combined strengths in reinsurance and capital markets.

“The issuance marks significant progress gained for Hong Kong’s insurance industry and capital markets in risk transfer and the use of alternative capital under the support of our country. It will further enhance the market’s capacity to manage catastrophe and other specialty risks, and consolidate Hong Kong’s position as an international risk management centre.

“This will enable us to unleash the synergy effect of multilayered risk transfer and pooling mechanisms through ILS and other tools, thus consolidating our strategic role as a regional and global catastrophe and specialty risk management hub.

“ILS and captive insurance, which we have long been promoting, can provide enterprises ‘going global’ with diversified means of spreading and managing risks.

“We expect this combination of financial policy measures will allow enterprises to leverage Hong Kong as a safe haven for ‘going global’ with greater ease of mind.”

Clement Cheung, Chief Executive Officer of the Insurance Authority added, “Riding on policy support from the National Financial Regulatory Administration, this ILS issuance fully demonstrates the commitment and determination with which we pursue the development of Hong Kong into a global risk management centre.

“The IA will also sustain efforts to facilitate introduction of protected cell company as an ILS structure and review the existing definition of eligible ILS investors for a more vibrant trading market.”

Now that we understand this new Great Wall Re insurance-linked securities arrangement for PICC P&C is a quota share reinsurance sidecar deal we have removed it from our catastrophe bond Deal Directory and added it to our directory of reinsurance sidecar transactions.

It’s encouraging to see the expansion of Hong Kong’s ILS regime to incorporate sidecar arrangements and also good to see the unique use-case to cover offshore wind power risks in China.

Find details of numerous reinsurance sidecar investments and transactions, including life reinsurance sidecar structures, in our directory of collateralized reinsurance sidecar transactions.

Casualty insurance-linked securities transactions are complex and require strong alignment, which makes finding strategic partners and understanding their motivations key, while at the same time given the complexity of arrangements such as casualty sidecars, realistic timelines are important, Philippe Trahan of Calidris Investment Partners said yesterday.

Trahan, Co-founder and Co-CEO of insurance-focused investment manager Calidris Investment Partners, was speaking during a casualty ILS focused panel session at the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference yesterday.

As a company with a focus on opportunities in these longer-tailed areas of insurance and reinsurance, Trahan noted that Calidris recognises the time required to both get comfortable with counterparties and asset managers involved in casualty transactions, as well as being cognisant of the time needed to get to well-structured and aligned deal outcomes.

“What we spend a lot of time on, we’re really more focused on finding partners, establishing strategic partnerships. What we want to avoid is we don’t want to be a hedge. So therefore motivations as to why, whether it’s an MGA or broker facility these days, an insurer or reinsurer that is considering wanting to launch a sidecar, why is it that they’re doing it, and what are their motivations?,” Trahan explained.

“What I find is then, it’s a bit of a different approach. I would say it’s a market that was mostly done on a bilateral basis between investors and counterparties, and so this year with the kind of syndicated market, which is a normal and natural evolution, it actually shows that it’s growing, it has legs.

“It does bring some additional complexity, and there’s a realisation that’s required on the broker or counterparty side. Once you’re comfortable that their motivations are trying to strive to achieve a partnership, that will ideally be scalable and repeatable, these require a lot of time from the management suite. So they don’t do this for a one-year trade and just disappear. So that’s quite helpful.”

He went on to suggest that timelines need to be realistic, as the complexity and work-effort involved in casualty ILS deals means that they are unlikely to be completed particularly quickly.

Trahan said, “The other obstacle is, we find, unrealistic timelines. These sidecars take six to 12 months to do, and anyone that comes now with a sidecar wanting to do it by year end, that’s wholly unrealistic timelines in my view, there’s a fair amount of diligence that’s required.”

There also needs to be an understanding of the additional complexities that go into structuring and creating a transaction that needs to take into account both the insurance liabilities and asset management sides of the equation.

Trahan continued, “There’s a lot of discussion you have with the other side, that is either the securities team of a broker or generally with counterparties, that if they discussed ILS markets in the past, they probably discussed using cash, T-bills as collateral. So starting to discuss CLOs and rated feeder notes, that generally tends to bring a different group within that organisation, or you only end up working with bigger organisations. Or if you’re dealing with an MGA group, you bring fronters into the mix, and that just makes things more complex and just takes more time. That’s another dynamic, another element that we find.”

Trahan also discussed the critical importance of alignment in casualty ILS transactions, highlighting that expectations need to be set, particularly around alignment on both the potential upside and downside of any partnership arrangement on casualty risks.

He explained, “The last element I would point to is willingness for counterparties to share in the upside and the downside. So having to further strengthen the alignment, sliding scale commissions for example is one of those elements that just show more alignment. Because ultimately they’ll know their book way better than we will.

“We’ll spend a lot of time discussing how you come with that view, and then we’ll build in a slide around it. This is not me or you trying to see whether I have a different view, a lower view of your loss ratio, so there’s an asymmetric transaction that takes place. That’s not how we think of it, so that requires more time as well.”

Trahan’s comments all speak to the complexity of casualty risks and the structural innovation that has come about through the use of insurance-linked securities technology to enable investors to participate in these areas of insurance.

They also highlight the need for a disciplined approach and a willingness to fully-engage with partners on transactions, to avoid any unexpected or uncertain outcomes.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

At the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference today, Karen Clark, CEO and Co-founder of catastrophe risk modelling specialist Karen Clark & Company, urged the insurance-linked securities community and its investors to ask for alternative model views to be included in the deal flow that comes to market.

During a panel discussion about how catastrophe modelling can be reimagined, Clark highlighted that ILS deal flow is typically concentrated around views of risk from the main vendor models.

As technology advancements, next-generation models, artificial intelligence and new data sources are increasingly being adopted across insurance and reinsurance, Clark feels the industry would be well-served by more models getting into the offering documents and ILS deal analysis process.

She said that, at KCC, they already have a significant market penetration with primary insurers in the United States, but often these companies need to use a model that may not be the one they use for most of their internal analysis, when it comes to catastrophe bonds or ILS deals.

“It’s actually ironic, because they use our models for their own rate making, pricing, underwriting, reinsurance, exposure management. So they’re using our models for everything they do internally, and then the brokers like to use the incumbents, as you would say, the two I call the old models for various reasons,” she explained.

Continuing to state that, “It creates a problem. We do remodel the cat bonds for many investors. We do give the KCC view, so the KCC view is accepted. We’ve had insurers who have wanted to, they use our models for everything else, they wanted to use it for their cat bond, but the brokers and the deal managers said no, we can’t use another model, the investors won’t accept it, it’s just not going to go well. And they scare these companies that they can’t use it.

“I think one of the things is, investors need to speak up that you do value alternative views, second generation models. We don’t have to keep getting the same old, same old.”

Clearly Clark has a vested interest to push this idea, it would be wrong not to mention that.

But, the question of how to get more views of risk into the catastrophe bond and ILS deal process is one that comes up a lot in discussions with market participants and many in the ILS community would welcome a broader range of views on transactions.

As risk models become increasingly capable, we should expect new views of risk to become accepted within the ILS market. Many alternative views of risk are already being used and ILS managers typically adopt numerous sources of analysis and data.

Clark further said that the main vendor models used in the ILS market won’t have as much incentive to change, if they don’t see more competition in the ILS deal making process.

Later during the panel discussion Clark said, “What I think would be very useful for the market is, if we could have in the OC’s, in the documentation, multi-model views and even more importantly, more data disclosure.”

Saying that, what this would mean for ILS investors is, “The decision that will be changed is which contracts you’re putting more of your capital on, which ones are actually better, better modelled, have better data. The more data you have, the less uncertainty you have about that. The decision is really with how you’re going to construct your portfolio, what are the contracts that are going to be in your portfolio because we have better information.

“Tell the deal managers, the brokers that you want to see alternative models in these transactions.”

ILS investors need to speak up and ask for alternative model views: Karen Clark was published by: www.Artemis.bm

Verisk, a catastrophe risk modelling and data analytics specialist, has now issued an initial industry insured loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion.

Verisk’s initial industry loss estimate includes losses from wind and privately insured storm surge, as a result of hurricane Isaias’ landfall in the Florida Panhandle.

The company added that wind damages are expected to account for the vast majority of insured losses from the storm.

Verisk further said that its estimate includes losses to onshore residential, commercial and industrial properties and automobiles for building, contents and time-element coverages, with modeled scenarios that incorporate losses from wind and storm surge.

The company expects that losses from precipitation-induced flooding will not be a significant factor with Isaias.

Commenting on the damages seen, Verisk added, “The most severe wind damage occurred west of Isaias’ landfall location, particularly in Florida’s Santa Rosa and northeastern Escambia counties. Reported impacts included roof damage, structural damage, downed trees and widespread debris. In Okaloosa County, the most common damage mechanism was trees falling onto residential structures. Overall, the event was characterized primarily by wind-related damage, including fallen trees, damaged roofs, fencing losses and debris impacts.

“Power outages were widespread across the Florida Panhandle, with some counties reporting outages affecting a majority of residents. Additional impacts were reported in Alabama and Georgia, where the weakening storm and its remnants caused downed trees and further power disruptions.”

This first initial insurance market loss estimate for hurricane Isaias from Verisk is one of the lower available so far, although within the anticipated low to mid single digit billion range.

As we reported earlier, Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion.

Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range.

Specialist insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager Leadenhall Capital Partners LLP is monitoring investor appetite for different ILS products, while leveraging artificial intelligence to increase productivity and improve its risk analysis, CEO Luca Albertini told Artemis.

Launched in 2008, Leadenhall Capital Partners has built a proven track-record across the ILS market, with strategies focused on reinsurance opportunities, catastrophe bonds, life and alternative credit insurance linked investments.

During a recent interview with Artemis around the key conference season, Luca Albertini, CEO and one of the founders of the firm, discussed how he hopes to differentiate Leadenhall to attract clients through the rest of 2026 and into 2027.

“We hope investors will see in Leadenhall an established player (we launched in 2008) with access to a deep pool of experience underwriting skills, with a stable senior management team and the support of a large multinational financial services group (MSI), whilst maintaining independence in the investment decisions and a corporate structure (partnership) which strongly aligns the investment team with the interest of our investors,” Albertini told Artemis.

Expanding further on this, the CEO then detailed what opportunities he currently sees within the market that Leadenhall can use to grow its business further into 2027 and beyond.

“Leadenhall has seen a significant growth in its AUM in 2026, whilst remaining focused on its core offering,” Albertini said.

He continued: “The team has capacity to further grow its current offering, but we constantly monitor investor appetite for different products and we assess the opportunity in line with our view of the medium term potential for those opportunities and our own skills set needed to underwrite the underlying products.”

Addressing the firm’s technology roadmap, Albertini highlighted how Leadenhall is adopting a measured approach to artificial intelligence, balancing enterprise-wide adoption with strict oversight.

“Leadenhall has invested in AI, and is currently having business access to one leading platform . Each team and each function in the firm is challenged to think how to use AI to increase productivity and improve our ability to analyse risk,” the Leadenhall Capital Partners CEO said.

Concluding: “We are doing this however in a controlled way and lots of attention is also put on “hallucinations” and on the quality of the output, so the validation of what AI generates remains key.”

Speaking ahead of the 2026 Baden-Baden gathering, Leopoldo Camara, Head of P&C Reinsurance Northern, Central & Eastern Europe at Swiss Re outlined that more reinsurance capital is needed in the market to address growing, interconnected risks, while also emphasising that the reinsurer will use its deep risk expertise to align alternative capital where it makes sense.

“We see more capital flowing into the markets and into the reinsurance industry, and we think that is actually good news because more capital is needed to address the growing risks that we all need to deal with,” Camara explained.

Moreover, Camara underscored that different types of capital play different roles across the industry, highlighting the company’s long-standing commitment to reinsurance and its combination of capital with deep risk expertise.

“Our capital, the Swiss Re capital, is committed to the industry for a very long time. It is here to do multi-line reinsurance. So, we do life and health and P&C, we do short tail and long tail,” the executive said.

“The core business proposition of our capital, the core mandate is on the right side of the balance sheet. So, we’re here to play to pay claims. That’s our main promise: paying claims,” Camara continued.

“And we issue this promise, bringing alongside capital, deep risk expertise that we have acquired over more than 100 years. And this deep risk expertise, in our view, is absolutely indispensable to arrange risk transfer in a sustainable way, to help mitigate the risk, to actually measure and quantify the risk, to develop new risk transfer approaches, and also to align alternative capital when this makes sense.

“So, this is our kind of capital. That’s the kind of capital we’re bringing to Baden-Baden, and we actually see that our capital is in high demand.”

On the demand side, Camara noted that Swiss Re was seeing increasing amounts of systemic risk, with exposures becoming more interconnected and therefore more systemic.

The executive identified four key factors driving this trend: larger individual risks, intensified geographic clustering, enhanced integration of supply chain networks, and growing digital and social networks that amplify risk propagation.

“Larger individual risks, the prime example that comes to mind are data centers, where we see insured value concentrations in excess of billions, sometimes even tens of billions, in very small, limited locations. So, increasing amounts of large risk concentration,” Camara added.

Going back to alternative capital, Camara highlighted during the Q&A portion of the briefing, that Swiss Re has a long-standing track record in the space, through the use of its third-party capital markets focused Alternative Capital Partners (ACP) division.

“Swiss Re has a long-standing track record in a unit called Alternative Capital Partners. So we’re quite used and experienced in also deploying that kind of capital or supporting that kind of capital with what we bring to the table to enable alternative capital to actually take on risk,” the executive said.

At the 2026 Monte Carlo Rendez-Vous de Septembre (RVS) reinsurance industry event, Urs Baertschi, Chief Executive Officer, of P&C Reinsurance, underscored the importance of the reinsurers Alternative Capital Partners division, whilst also stating that Swiss Re expects to continue to be a “meaningful participant in that market.”
